va_grayson_highlands_state_park.blurb: A high-country boulder park in the mountains of far southwest Virginia, set within a state park that adjoins the Mount Rogers recreation area. Almost every problem here is bouldering, and the range is wide: from very easy lines through to V12 and V13, with the bulk of the problems between V0 and V6. The boulders mostly sit between about 4,500 and 4,900 feet, with open views, and the Highlands zone climbs higher still. Much of the stone is rhyolite, dark with pink feldspar, and it is sharp and steep, favouring crimps, edges, pinches and flakes. Big boulders with fairly low landings are typical. Summer is the draw, when it stays cool, and September is a standout; winter is harsh. The largest groupings are Boneyard, Listening Rock Trail, Haw Orchard and the Picnic Area.

bc_west_kootenay.blurb: Climbing spread across southeastern British Columbia, centred on Nelson, Castlegar and the Slocan Valley. Bouldering makes up the largest share, followed by sport and then trad, with a handful of alpine lines in the Valhalla range. Sport routes cluster around 5.9 to 5.12, trad runs a similar spread, and the boulders cover everything from V0 up to V9, with the majority in the easier and middle grades. The stone is good-quality granite and gneiss, and roped routes run from single pitches up to about eight. Rope climbing generally runs from April to October, drier than Squamish and cooler than Skaha. For bouldering, autumn is the prime window, when many south-facing blocks dry quickly. Castlegar and Nelson are the biggest hubs, with Slocan Valley close behind.

bc_skaha_bluffs.blurb: A hillside of cliffs overlooking Skaha Lake, just south of Penticton in the Okanagan, with the climbing arranged along three parallel canyons. This is first and foremost a sport climbing destination, with a smaller trad contingent, and the grades lean hard: most routes fall between 5.10 and 5.12, with a modest supply of moderates in the 5.6 to 5.9 range and a few above 5.13. The rock is coarse-grained gneiss, and the cliffs are mostly under 30 metres, so routes are single-pitch or short. The area is known for mild weather. It is split into many walls and groups, among them Evergreen Drive Crags, the Southern Crags, White Walls, Doctors' Group, Red Tail Group and The Fortress, so a visit can easily fill several days.

co_eldorado_canyon_state_park.blurb: A narrow canyon in Boulder County, just southwest of Boulder, whose sandstone walls rise as high as 700 feet. Traditional multi-pitch climbing rules here: delicate face climbing, dihedrals and irregular cracks, protected with gear you place yourself, with only a sprinkling of sport routes and limited top roping. Grades stretch from easy routes to 5.13, but the weight sits from about 5.8 to 5.12, and there is also a separate bouldering collection. Weather turns quickly, with spring snowstorms, high winds and summer afternoon thunderstorms. Fixed gear can be unreliable, so a helmet and solid judgement matter. The biggest formations include Redgarden Wall, the West Ridge, the Bastille and Wind Tower, with plenty of smaller crags between them.

az_queen_creek_canyon.blurb: A volcanic canyon about an hour east of Phoenix, just north of Superior, with the climbing scattered across many separate crags from Oak Flat to Devil's Canyon. Sport routes are the largest group, then bouldering, then a smaller trad set. The cliffs and spires are welded tuff with good friction, mostly solid but friable or hollow in spots; expect featured faces, sharp crimps, pockets and some lower-angle slabs. Rope climbs run from moderate up to 5.13, with the heaviest concentration at 5.9 to 5.12, while the boulders are mostly V0 to V5 with a tail of harder problems. Devil's Canyon has plenty of routes, but its lower grades can be sandbagged with longer gaps between bolts. Other big groups include Euro Dog Valley, Atlantis and the Mine Area.

tx_austin_area.blurb: A cluster of climbing spots in and around Austin, in central Texas, ranging from city-edge cliffs to ranch and park crags. Sport routes lead, bouldering is close behind, and there is a smaller amount of top rope and trad plus some deep-water soloing at Pace Bend. Sport grades are centred on 5.10 to 5.12 with a decent number of easier lines; boulders mostly sit between V0 and V8. The rock at most of the crags is limestone. Barton Creek Greenbelt is the nearest, about eight minutes from downtown and with many routes suited to beginners, while Reimers Ranch lies roughly 45 minutes west above the Pedernales River, with a newer North Shore sector. McKinney Falls is mainly bouldering with stiffer grades. Climbers favour temperatures of about 40 to 60 degrees Fahrenheit, since summer can be punishing without shade.
